name: Vamanapureeswarar Temple, Thirumanikuzhi
deity: Shiva as Vamanapureeswarar (Udhavi Nayagar), with the Goddess Ambujakshi (Udhavi Nayaki)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu on the Kedilam, sung by Sambandar (7th century); Chola inscriptions
summary: Beside the Kedilam near Cuddalore, Shiva keeps the shrine where Vishnu came as the boy Vamana to worship him — and where a screen bearing Bheema Rudra still guards that worship from interruption.

sections.history: Thirumanikuzhi is a village on the Kedilam river in Cuddalore district, about 10 km west of Cuddalore on the road to Panruti. Its temple to Shiva as Vamanapureeswarar is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted among the shrines of Nadu Nadu. Thirugnana Sambandar sang its Lord in a pathigam, calling the place Udhavi Manikkuzhi — a name the temple's inscriptions also keep, for here Shiva is remembered as Udhavi Nayagar, the Lord who came to help. Inscriptions of the Chola period, including records of Rajaraja I and Kulothunga I, show the shrine honoured and endowed by the great Chola kings. It is administered today by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
sections.architecture: The temple covers about two acres, its shrines enclosed within concentric rectangular walls, and it is entered from the east through a five-tiered rajagopuram. The sanctum of Vamanapureeswarar is unusual: before the lingam hangs a cloth screen bearing the image of Bheema Rudra, one of the eleven Rudras, and worship is offered first to the screen. The shrine of the Goddess Ambujakshi faces north in the first precinct.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Vishnu, after taking the form of Vamana to humble the generous king Mahabali, came here as a young brahmachari — a maani — and worshipped Shiva to be cleansed; the place took its name, Thirumanikuzhi, from him. Vishnu prayed that his worship should never be disturbed, and Shiva set Bheema Rudra to guard it, which is why the screen still stands before the sanctum. Another tradition tells of a merchant from the north set upon by robbers, who cried out to Shiva and was rescued — and so the Lord and the Goddess are called Udhavi Nayagar and Udhavi Nayaki.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri in the Tamil month of Masi and Navaratri in Purattasi are the principal festivals, with the monthly pradosham and the customary Shaiva observances of the year; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: The moment to wait for here is the deeparadhana, when the Bheema Rudra screen is drawn aside and the lingam is seen in the lamplight, briefly, before the curtain falls again. Thirumanikuzhi pairs naturally with Thiruvahindrapuram's Devanatha Perumal Temple, a short way downstream on the same river, and with Thirupathiripuliyur in Cuddalore town.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Thirumanikuzhi lies about 10 km west of Cuddalore on the Cuddalore–Panruti road, with frequent buses. Cuddalore and Tiruppadiripuliyur have railway stations, with Villupuram the nearest major junction; Puducherry has the closest airport, and Chennai the nearest major international airport.
